c.tagline: The Pearl of the Atlantic — 27 beaches where São Paulo comes up for air

card: Visa/Mastercard widely accepted at hotels, mid-range restaurants, and shops in Pitangueiras/Enseada; carry cash (R$) for beach kiosks (quiosques), small vendors, buses, and taxis, which often don't take cards

taxi.color: White (standard São Paulo state livery, unlike Rio's yellow cabs)
taxi.fareNote: Metered (taxímetro); a short beachfront hop runs R$15-30 (~$3-6); ride-hailing apps are usually cheaper and easier

emergency.note: Fire/rescue: 193; Municipal Guard (GCM) tourist support: 153. Main beach zones see heavy summer police presence; petty theft (phone/bag snatching) on crowded beaches is the top risk

walk: The main beach strip (Pitangueiras-Astúrias-Enseada) is flat and highly walkable along a continuous beachfront calçadão (promenade), but Guarujá stretches over 25km of coastline, so reaching outlying beaches like Tombo, Guaiúba, or Góes requires a bus, taxi, or rideshare.

safety.safety: The core tourist beach zones (Pitangueiras, Enseada, Astúrias, Tombo, Pernambuco) are generally safe by day and evening, with visible police/GCM patrols during summer high season; the biggest realistic risk is petty theft on crowded sand.
safety.crime: Some inland/outskirt neighborhoods (parts of Vicente de Carvalho, Vila Baiana, Sítio Conceiçãozinha) have higher rates of drug-trafficking-related violent crime and are not tourist areas — solo travelers should stick to the beachfront districts and avoid wandering into unfamiliar inland streets after dark.

hood_landmark.Pitangueiras: Praia das Pitangueiras & Rua Mário Ribeiro
hood_landmark.Enseada: Praia da Enseada (5.6 km waterfront promenade)
hood_landmark.Pernambuco: Mar Casado & Fortaleza de Santo Amaro da Barra Grande

avoid.reason: Caution in hillside (morro) communities away from the beaches

hood_desc: The bustling heart of Guarujá — a lively central beach lined with shopping galleries, bars, and the city's densest cluster of restaurants, all steps from the sand.
Guarujá's longest beach at 5.6km, backed by the biggest concentration of hotels and everyday commerce — markets, pharmacies, casual eateries — making it the practical, family-friendly base.
A calmer, more traditional stretch beside Pitangueiras, prized for gentle waters, family appeal, and the photogenic rocky outcrops framing the shoreline.
An upscale, tree-lined enclave of gated condos and golf courses where two beaches merge at low tide (Mar Casado); Guarujá's most exclusive, tranquil address.
A Blue Flag-certified beach favored by surfers and a younger crowd, with an energetic strip of bars overlooking the swell — Guarujá's closest thing to a nightlife district.
lodging: Jequitimar Guarujá Resort & Spa by Accor

water.note: Tap water is treated, but most visitors and many locals stick to bottled or filtered.

transit.sys: City Mais municipal buses (successor to COOPERGUARU) cover the beaches and inland neighborhoods
transit.hours: ~5am-midnight on most routes, reduced late-night frequency
transit.pay: Cash or rechargeable Bilhete Único card, roughly R$4.40-4.90 (~$0.90-1) per ride
transit.map: No unified live-tracking app; check Moovit or the Prefeitura de Guarujá transport page for routes/schedules
transit.note: The classic scenic alternative is the balsa (ferry) to/from Santos rather than a bus

transport.air: No commercial airport in Guarujá itself; nearest options are São Paulo's Guarulhos Intl (GRU) and Congonhas (CGH), each roughly 90km / 1.5-2.5 hrs by road via the Rodovia dos Imigrantes/Anchieta
transport.train: No direct passenger rail link; travelers connect via São Paulo's metro/CPTM to a bus terminal, then bus or car onward
transport.bus: Frequent intercity coaches run from São Paulo's Tietê and Jabaquara terminals to Guarujá's rodoviária, about 1.5-2 hrs and roughly $10-20
transport.ferry: The Santos-Guarujá balsa crosses the Porto de Santos channel every 15-30 minutes, ~24 hours a day; free for pedestrians and cyclists, R$12.30 for cars
transport.car: Via the Rodovia dos Imigrantes/Anchieta from São Paulo (~80km, 1-1.5 hrs outside rush hour), then the ferry or the coastal SP-055 highway

airport.name: São Paulo/Guarulhos Intl (GRU) or São Paulo/Congonhas (CGH)
airport.transport: Private transfer/taxi ~$90-110 one-way (CGH); intercity bus via Jabaquara ~$10-19; rental car ~1h10 self-drive

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage from Vivo, Claro, and TIM across the main beach areas; can weaken in inland/hilly pockets
net.w: Free Wi-Fi common in hotels, cafes, and shopping areas; less reliable on the open beach
net.fwn: Available at many hotels, cafes, and malls (e.g., Praiamar Shopping); free public Wi-Fi is limited outside hotels/cafes
net.ap: A local prepaid SIM (Vivo/Claro/TIM kiosks) or an eSIM purchased before arrival is advisable for reliable data and Uber/99 use

tip.s: 10% service charge is often included on restaurant bills as 'taxa de serviço' (technically optional, generally paid); round up for taxis and small tips for bellhops/informal beach service are appreciated but not obligatory
tip.r: If service isn't included, 10% is standard; nothing extra is expected at casual quiosques

landmarks: Praia da Enseada
Guarujá's sweeping main bay unfurls nearly six kilometers of golden sand backed by hotels, kiosks and calm surf, making it the city's liveliest seaside playground.
Praia de Pitangueiras
The downtown beach where Guarujá began, fronted by shops and high-rises, offers gentle waves, buzzing promenades and easy access to the island's best people-watching.
Fortaleza da Barra Grande
A 16th-century Portuguese fortress guarding the Santos channel entrance, reachable by boat or trail, rewards visitors with cannons, colonial walls and sweeping estuary views.
Morro do Maluf (Maluf Hill viewpoint)
This grassy headland between Pitangueiras and Enseada beaches serves up Guarujá's classic postcard panorama, especially dramatic when big swells explode against the rocks below.
Praia do Tombo
A Blue Flag-certified surfing beach with steep shore break and bohemian energy, Tombo draws wave riders and sunset photographers to its clean, compact crescent.
Praia do Éden (Eden Beach)
Hidden at the end of a jungle staircase, this tiny emerald cove framed by rainforest and boulders feels like a secret slice of untouched tropical Brazil.
Acqua Mundo Aquarium
One of South America's largest aquariums plunges visitors among sharks, penguins and Amazonian fish, a family favorite steps from Enseada's sands.
Praia Branca (White Beach, Bertioga Channel)
Reached by boat or forest trail from Perequê, this rustic fishing-village beach on the Bertioga channel charms with caiçara culture, clear water and utter tranquility.
Praia do Perequê
Guarujá's working fishing village lines this long beach with colorful boats and seafood shacks, where the day's catch lands straight onto your lunch plate.
Mirante da Campina (Campina Hill Lookout)
Crowning one of the island's highest points, this hang-gliding launch and lookout delivers a 360-degree sweep over Guarujá's beaches, rainforest and the shimmering Atlantic.

train.note: No passenger railway serves Guarujá. Brazil has no intercity passenger trains, and the Santos lines nearby carry freight to the port. Arrive by coach from São Paulo or by the ferry across the Santos channel.

bus.note: No international coaches. Cometa and Ultra run from São Paulo's Jabaquara terminal to Guarujá in about 90 minutes via the Imigrantes motorway; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). Weekend and holiday traffic down the Serra do Mar can double the journey time.

intl.to: Santos - Ponta da Praia (Brazil) - ~10 min across the channel, 24 hr

ferry.note: There are no international sailings, but the little Santos-Guarujá car and passenger ferry across the harbour channel is real transport, running around the clock and saving a long drive around the estuary. Queues for vehicles get very long on summer weekends; foot passengers walk straight on. The crossing takes about ten minutes.

half.name: Santos
half.blurb: Port city with the world's longest beachfront garden, a funicular up Monte Serrat, and a museum dedicated to Pelé.

half.name: São Paulo
half.blurb: Brazil's largest city, with museums, Avenida Paulista, and a historic center reachable from the coast by highway.

full.name: São Sebastião
full.blurb: Colonial coastal town on the mainland opposite Ilhabela, with a preserved historic center and calm beaches.

full.name: Ilhabela
full.blurb: Mostly undeveloped island reached by ferry, covered in Atlantic rainforest with waterfalls and dozens of beaches.

full.name: Ubatuba
full.blurb: Coastal town with more than 100 beaches along a stretch of protected Atlantic rainforest coastline.
